questions.explain: Only INC001 has both priority 1 and assigned false. INC002 is priority 1 but assigned true; INC003 is unassigned but priority 2, not 1.

questions.q: In the filter callback `return ticket.priority === 1 && ticket.assigned === false;`, what happens if a ticket has `priority: 1` but `assigned: true`?
options: It passes the filter, because priority matches
It fails the filter, because && requires both conditions to be true, and assigned === false is not
It is automatically converted to assigned: false
questions.explain: && only returns true when both sides are true. priority === 1 is true, but assigned === false is false here, so the overall condition is false and the ticket is excluded.

questions.q: After `.filter()` runs but before `.map()` runs, what does the intermediate array (unassignedCritical) contain?
options: An array of just the ticket number strings
An array of the full ticket objects that passed the filter condition
The original, unfiltered array of all tickets
questions.explain: filter narrows the array down but doesn't reshape its items - it still holds the full ticket objects, not just their numbers. map is the step that extracts just the number property.

questions.q: Why does the function use `===` instead of `==` when comparing `ticket.priority === 1`?
options: === is required syntax for filter callbacks
There is no actual difference between them here
== would cause a syntax error inside filter
To deliberately avoid type coercion, since priority should already be a real number - === checks type and value together
questions.explain: === avoids the silent type coercion that == performs, matching the strict-equality habit this course recommends throughout.

questions.q: If you wanted to know how many tickets matched, in addition to their numbers, which approach fits the pattern used in this lesson?
options: Call .length on the original tickets array
Call .length on the array returned by .filter(), before .map() reshapes it down to just numbers
Count manually with a separate loop, since filter doesn't produce something you can measure
questions.explain: .filter() already returns a real array, so .length on that intermediate result gives the match count with no extra logic needed.
